planting.note: Set out grafted or air-layered trees in spring once the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; young trees need cold protection for their first two winters.

directions: Grow in full sun on deep, well-drained soil that can be sandy, rocky, or calcareous; 'Prolific' is valued by South Florida growers chiefly for its dependable, heavy annual crops of small to medium round fruit rather than for exceptional size. The grainy tan flesh has the classic malty, brown-sugar sweetness typical of good sapodilla selections, and the tree bears at a relatively young age for a grafted cultivar. Because it sets fruit so heavily, thinning is rarely needed but trees benefit from occasional light fertilization during the growing season to sustain production. Like other sapodilla cultivars it is highly drought- and wind-tolerant once established and is best reserved for zone 10-11 or the warmest protected pockets of zone 9b, since young wood is damaged below the low 30s F.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sapodilla Cultivars for Florida
California Rare Fruit Growers — Sapodilla Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; reserve for zone 10-11 or the warmest microclimates of 9b and shield young trees from cold their first two winters.

directions: Named for the ancient Maya city in Guatemala within the species' native range, 'Tikal' is a Central American sapodilla selection grown in South Florida for its good-quality, medium-sized fruit with fine-grained, sweet, brown-sugar-flavored flesh and comparatively few grit cells. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; the tree is vigorous and productive once established, tolerating the alkaline, rocky soils common to South Florida plantings. As with all sapodilla, harvest fruit while still firm but showing the characteristic dull, scurfy skin, then let it soften at room temperature for several days before eating, since unripe fruit is astringent with latex. Mature trees withstand brief dips into the upper 20s F with only leaf damage, but young wood needs frost protection.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sapodilla Growing in the Florida Home Landscape

planting.note: Set out grafted trees in spring in a warm, full-sun location once frost risk has passed; protect young trees from cold for the first couple of winters in zone 9b-10 plantings.

directions: 'Makok' is a Thai sapodilla selection introduced to Florida collector orchards for its small, round, olive-shaped fruit borne in heavy clusters, distinct from the larger single fruits typical of most Florida cultivars. The flesh is smooth-textured, sweet, and low in grit, making it a favorite for fresh eating in Southeast Asian cuisine. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; the tree is moderately vigorous and, like other sapodilla selections, extremely tolerant of drought, wind, and salt once established. Fruit should be picked while still firm and allowed to ripen off the tree for several days at room temperature, since sapodilla harvested too early remains astringent with latex.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Sapodilla Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant seedlings or grafted stock in spring in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil; this large forest tree is slow to establish and is only suitable for the warmest zone 9b-10 microclimates or long-term container culture farther north.

directions: Manilkara chicle is the classic wild chicle tree of the lowland rain forests of Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala, historically tapped by chicleros for its milky latex, which was the original base ingredient of natural chewing gum before synthetic substitutes took over the industry. It is closely related to sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) and produces similar small, brown-skinned, sweet fruit with grainy, malty-flavored flesh, though it is grown far more often as a massive forest timber and latex tree than as a dooryard fruit crop. In cultivation it wants full sun and deep, well-drained, fertile soil, and rewards patience with a very long-lived, wind-firm, drought-tolerant canopy tree once established. Because of its eventual great size, it is best suited to large properties or naturalistic plantings rather than small home gardens, and young trees need frost protection in any zone cooler than the tropical range they evolved in.
sources: Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates
